title: Gleaning (Ruth 2–4)
hook: Boaz leaves extra grain on purpose, and Ruth becomes David's great-grandmother

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth's chesed on the road to Bethlehem: whither thou goest, I will go. Your line was thy people, my people.

There's no food in the house. Naomi and Ruth have reached Bethlehem with nothing, just as the barley harvest begins. So Ruth does what the poor did in Israel: she goes out behind the reapers and picks up what they drop. The law of Moses said farmers must not strip their fields bare; leave the edges and what falls for the poor and the stranger, a safety net built into the harvest. Ruth is both poor and a stranger. And the field she happens to walk into belongs to Boaz, Booz in the Douay-Rheims, a relative of Naomi's dead husband.
screen: `NO FOOD IN THE HOUSE.` → `LEAVE THE EDGES FOR THE POOR.` → `A FIELD THAT BELONGS TO BOAZ.`

segments.voice: Gleaning means gathering what's left after the harvest: the stray ears of grain, the leftovers, the edges. It's slow, bent-over work, the work of people with nothing else. Boaz walks out, sees the foreign woman, and asks who she is. He's already heard everything she did for her mother-in-law. So he protects her: stay in my field, drink from my workers' water jars, eat with us at mealtime. Then he quietly tells his young men, in the Douay: "let fall some of your handfuls of purpose, and leave them, that she may gather them without shame." Of purpose. He doesn't hand her a sack of grain like a charity case. He arranges the field so her own work finds more, and her dignity stays whole. That evening she beats out about an ephah of barley. In the chapters that follow, Naomi sends Ruth to Boaz at the threshing floor, and Boaz acts as the go'el, the kinsman who redeems a family's land and name. He marries Ruth. They have a son, Obed. And the book ends with a short family tree: Obed is the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David. A foreign widow who gathered leftovers becomes the great-grandmother of King David. Catholics hear one more step: when Matthew's Gospel opens with Jesus's family tree, Ruth is named in it, one of only a few women listed. Kindness on purpose, in one barley field, runs all the way to Bethlehem again.
screen: `GLEANING — GATHERING WHAT'S LEFT.` · `LET FALL SOME HANDFULS ON PURPOSE.` · `BOAZ, THE KINSMAN WHO REDEEMS.` · `GREAT-GRANDMOTHER OF DAVID.` · then, large: `THAT SHE MAY GATHER THEM WITHOUT SHAME.`

segments.voice: Think about where your own field has edges: the extra in the grocery cart, the tip, the parking spot near the door, the credit for an idea. Pick one place you could let something fall on purpose, so someone else can pick it up without feeling handed charity, and picture doing it quietly, the way Boaz did. If you pray, ask for eyes like his.
Gleaning. Gathering the grain left behind after harvest, which the law left for the poor and the stranger. Ruth gleaned in the field of Boaz. Today's word.
Your line: kindness on purpose. Boaz made sure it looked like her own harvest. Day three hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Ruth's story in the weekday Mass readings, and some Catholic charities and parish food ministries point to gleaning as a model of caring for the poor while protecting their dignity.
